title: ‘Crocodiles are possible, but hunger is certain’: Malawi’s foragers forced into infested waters

Coated in grey, foul-smelling mud up to her thighs, the 34-year-old mother of four plunges both arms deep into the heavy sediment of a sprawling marsh. Her fingers feel blindly through the silt for the rough, bulbous roots of wild water lilies, known as nyika . Around her, a dozen other women move with deliberate, hushed slowness. No one splashes; no one speaks above a tense whisper. Just 50 yards away, where the marsh opens into the main artery of the Shire River, the silhouette of a Nile crocodile glides silently beneath the surface. “Every time you reach down into the mud, you wonder if your hand will come back up,” Maseko says. She spends up to five hours a day searching through these waters. The danger is not abstract. In the villages of Maseya and neighbouring Kasisi, in southern Malawi’s Chikwawa district, people talk about foragers who have gone into the deeper channels looking for larger roots and never returned. In 2024, Isaac Kenneth, a 28-year-old from a neighbouring settlement, was attacked while harvesting in the same stretch of water. The crocodile seized his leg and dragged him under. Fellow foragers managed to pull him free, but he suffered deep puncture wounds and a broken ankle. View image in fullscreen Families and foragers walk along an embankment beside the marshlands of the lower Shire River basin in Chikwawa, carrying the day’s harvest “The crocodile is a possibility, but hunger is a certainty,” Maseko says, hoisting a heavy wet sack on to her shoulder. “If I do not come into this water, my children will not eat tonight.” Nyika foraging is not new. For decades, communities in the lower Shire have harvested the tubers of the water lily ( Nymphaea petersiana ) during severe shortages, as documented in accounts from the 2005 food crisis and later lean seasons . What has changed is the scale and regularity. Once reserved for the worst drought years, the harvest has become weekly and commercial for many families across Malawi’s flood-prone southern lowlands, as extreme weather, weak support systems and rising food prices have combined to lock vulnerable households out of basic nutrition. View image in fullscreen Unpeeled wild water-lily bulbs. The starchy core requires lengthy boiling to reduce bitterness Every Monday and Thursday, the tracks leading to Sorgin Market fill with vendors carrying heavy wet bundles. Women sit on colourful cloths spread over the dry earth, surrounded by plastic basins piled high with mud-encrusted lily bulbs. For buyers priced out of the maize market, one basin can mean three days of basic survival for a family. The roots are boiled, dried and pounded into a gritty grey flour used to make porridge. The state-backed Agricultural Development and Marketing Corporation (Admarc) is mandated to buy maize from farmers at a fixed price to help steady markets and maintain emergency reserves. However, logistical bottlenecks, warehouse losses and funding shortfalls mean that cheaper public supplies are often heavily rationed or absent when communities need them most. In July, Admarc was selling maize at 39,500 kwacha (£17) for a 50kg bag. Sales were limited to a maximum of 20kg a person to prevent hoarding and resale. A small basin of nyika sells for roughly 2,500 Malawian kwacha (£1.10). With official reserves under strain, the only supplies of maize are on the open market, where prices swing wildly.
